title: Cheating Death
description: A jellyfish that runs its life backward, a centuries-old shark and a frog that freezes solid

concepts.title: The Jellyfish That Runs Its Life Backward
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1988 a German marine biology student, Christian Sommer, went snorkeling off the cliffs of Portofino in Italy and brought back hydroids, small colonial relatives of jellyfish. In the lab they released medusae, bell-shaped swimmers about the size of a little toenail. Then the medusae did something nobody expected: stressed, they sank to the bottom of the jar and turned back into baby polyps. His supervisor, Ferdinando Boero, called it "like a butterfly transforming back into a caterpillar." A 1996 paper reported that medusae at every stage, from newly released to fully mature, could do it, "thus escaping death and achieving potential immortality."1

Normally a hydrozoan's life runs one way: medusae release eggs and sperm, the larvae settle and grow into polyps, and the polyps bud off new medusae. When a Turritopsis dohrnii medusa is damaged, old or in poor conditions, it runs the cycle backward. It shrinks, settles and becomes a cyst, a shapeless ball of tissue, which within 24 to 36 hours starts sprouting a root-like stolon and new polyps. Along the way its cells transdifferentiate: instead of merely reverting within their own lineage, specialized cells switch to new cell types.2

Is it really immortal? Only in a narrow sense. A 2022 genome study called it immortal because mature medusae can rejuvenate with a probability of up to 100%, with no apparent limit on how many times.3 But that study compared it with a supposedly mortal cousin, Turritopsis rubra, and the jellyfish biologist Maria Pia Miglietta objected that earlier studies of a Japanese jellyfish, presumably T. rubra, found that it can rejuvenate too, only at a lower rate.4 And the trick is no defense against being eaten: the "immortal" jellyfish can still die from predation and disease.5

concepts.title: A Shark's Age, Read in Its Eyes
concepts.contentHtml:
The Greenland shark cruises the cold waters of the North Atlantic and the Arctic, and it does nothing in a hurry. Its body grows by only about a centimeter a year.1 Yet adults typically measure 4 to 5 meters, which makes it the largest fish native to Arctic waters, and at that pace the biggest must be very old. Proving it was hard. Fish are usually aged by counting growth layers in hard, calcified tissues, and this shark has none.

The answer was in its eyes. The core of a vertebrate's eye lens, the embryonic nucleus, is built before birth from metabolically inert proteins, so its carbon is as old as the animal. That carbon can be radiocarbon dated, and nuclear weapons tests from the mid-1950s added a handy time stamp: a "bomb pulse" of extra carbon-14 in the ocean's food web.2

In 2016 Julius Nielsen and colleagues dated the lens cores of 28 female sharks. Only the smallest, 220 centimeters long or less, carried the bomb pulse; the rest were born before it. The largest, at 502 centimeters, came out at 392 ± 120 years old, and females seem to reach sexual maturity only at 156 ± 22 years or more. Those ± figures are wide: each is the midpoint and half-width of a 95.4% probability range, so the record shark could be anywhere from about 272 to 512 years old. Even so, the team concluded that the Greenland shark is the longest-lived vertebrate known, and raised concerns about protecting a species that breeds so late.3

concepts.title: The Frog That Freezes Solid
concepts.contentHtml:
The wood frog is one of the few vertebrates that can survive being frozen. Up to 70% of the water in its body turns to ice, and for weeks or months it shows no breathing, no heartbeat and no brain activity. Then it thaws and emerges unharmed.1

The freeze starts from outside. "Its skin gets frozen a little bit, and then ice penetrates into the frog through veins and arteries," says Kenneth Storey of Carleton University in Ottawa, who studies the frogs. Meanwhile the frog's liver pumps out huge amounts of glucose, which seeps everywhere, including into the cells.2

That sugar is the trick. Ice forms outside the cells, and as it grows it pulls water out of them; a cell drained too far dries out and dies. Packed with glucose, the cells keep more of their water, a protection called cryoprotection.3 In spring the sugar-rich core organs, such as the liver and heart, melt first, so they can restart while the rest of the frog is still thawing.4

Alaska's wood frogs push the limits furthest. Researchers who tracked them to their winter hideouts in Interior Alaska found them frozen for 193 ± 11 days in a row, through temperatures as low as -18.1°C (about -1°F), and all 18 survived. Their tissues held far more glucose than frogs frozen in the lab, perhaps because repeated freezing and thawing in early autumn tops up the sugar each time.5

title: Bodies That Break the Rules
description: A cell with no mitochondria, anglerfish males that fuse to their mates, and the platypus

concepts.title: The Cell That Gave Up Its Mitochondria
concepts.contentHtml:
Mitochondria are often called the power plants of the cell, but they do more than make ATP: they help build and break down amino acids, fats and sugars, and help decide when a cell dies. Many single-celled organisms that live without oxygen have shrunk theirs into stripped-down versions. Even so, biologists thought every eukaryote (the group that includes animals, plants, fungi and protists) needed some form of mitochondrion, because of core jobs such as building iron-sulfur clusters, tiny bundles of iron and sulfur atoms that many proteins need to work.1

Then in 2016 a team led by Anna Karnkowska and Vladimír Hampl sequenced the genome of Monocercomonoides, a single-celled flagellate, and found none of the hallmark mitochondrial proteins. Even the mitochondrial machinery for iron-sulfur clusters, thought to be conserved in virtually all eukaryotic cells, was missing. In its place was a SUF system working in the main body of the cell, acquired from bacteria by lateral gene transfer. The family tree suggests it did not branch off before mitochondria arose: its ancestors had them, and it lost them.2

Swapping in that bacterial kit may be what made the loss possible, and a 2024 study confirmed that the SUF system really works.3 The organism, now named Monocercomonoides exilis, lives in the guts of chinchillas, where there is little oxygen to burn anyway. The genomes of two related gut flagellates show no reliable mitochondrial proteins either, which suggests the whole group, the oxymonads, gave up the organelle at least 100 million years ago. The claim rests on absence, so one convincing mitochondrial protein would overturn it. None has turned up yet.4

concepts.title: Anglerfish Males That Fuse for Life
concepts.contentHtml:
The deep sea is vast and dark, and male and female anglerfish rarely meet. Some species have solved this for good. A tiny male attaches himself to a female, their tissues fuse, and the two set up a common blood circulation, so he gets all his nutrients from her, like a donated organ in a transplant patient. The size gap can be staggering: in the most extreme cases, females are more than 60 times the length of the males and about half a million times as heavy.1

This sexual parasitism is rarer than its fame suggests. A 2005 review found permanently attached males in only 23 of the 160 known species of deep-sea anglerfish, and concluded that the habit evolved separately at least three and perhaps five or more times.2 One male Photocorynus spiniceps, fused to the back of a 46-millimeter female, is just 6.2 millimeters long, and in 2006 the anglerfish expert Ted Pietsch called it the smallest sexually mature vertebrate known. Its testes nearly fill its body, and depending on the family, a female may carry up to eight males.3

Fusing two individuals ought to trigger rejection, as a mismatched transplant does. A 2020 genetic study found that anglerfish species whose males attach only for a while have lost working aicda genes, which help antibodies sharpen their aim, and some permanently fusing species have even lost the rag genes behind the hallmark of adaptive immunity.4 "For humans, the combined loss of important immune facilities observed in anglerfishes would result in fatal immunodeficiency," said Thomas Boehm, the immunologist who led the project. The team concluded the fish rely on improved innate defenses instead, though the details remain to be discovered.5

concepts.title: The Platypus: Eggs, Venom and a Glow
concepts.contentHtml:
When the platypus was first described, many European naturalists thought the animal was a fake. It has fur and feeds its young on milk, yet with the echidnas it belongs to the monotremes, the mammals that lay eggs. A female lays one to three eggs and has no teats: the young suckle from two milk patches on her belly. Males carry a sharp spur about 12 millimeters long on each ankle, linked to a venom gland that is busiest in the breeding season. A jab from the spur will not kill a person, but the pain has been described as excruciating. Underwater, the platypus closes its eyes, ears and nostrils and finds food with its bill.1 That bill carries about 40,000 electroreceptors, which sense the weak electric currents made by the muscles of its prey.2

Its chromosomes are just as unusual. Most mammals have one pair of sex chromosomes, XX or XY. A male platypus has ten: five X and five Y, which link into a chain as sperm are made and then split into sperm carrying all five Xs or all five Ys. One end of the chain holds an X resembling the human X; near the other end sits one resembling the Z chromosome of birds.3

In 2020 came one more surprise. Under ultraviolet light, the brown fur of three museum platypuses glowed green to cyan, the first biofluorescence reported in a monotreme. With so few specimens, nobody can yet say whether the glow does anything for the animal.4

title: Cancers That Spread
description: Devil facial tumors, an ancient dog cancer, and clam leukemia that drifts through the sea

concepts.title: A Cancer Passed by Biting
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1996, in the northeast of Tasmania, Tasmanian devils began turning up with lumpy tumors on their faces and inside their mouths. The illness, devil facial tumor disease, passes between devils when they bite each other, spreads quickly through the body, and usually kills within months of the first signs.1

The strange part is what carries it. Tumors from devils across the island turned out to be genetically the same as each other and different from the animals carrying them: the cancer cells themselves are the infection, one line of cells that lives on in one host after another. The genes they switch on match those of Schwann cells, which wrap nerves in insulating myelin, so the cancer probably began in the nerves of a single devil.2 Cells from another animal are normally attacked and rejected, like a mismatched transplant. These cells get away with it partly by turning down the MHC molecules on their surface, the identity tags that immune cells check.3

The toll has been heavy. A 2021 study estimated that wild devils peaked at about 53,000 in 1996 and had fallen to about 17,000.4 Then came a second surprise. In 2014 and 2015, five devils in southern Tasmania had facial tumors that looked the same but were a different cancer altogether. The new one, DFT2, carries a Y chromosome, so it began in a male; the original began in a female. Devils have now produced at least two contagious cancers.5

concepts.title: The Cancer That Outlived Its Dog
concepts.contentHtml:
Thousands of years ago, a dog developed a tumor. That dog is long gone, but its cancer is not: its cells are still alive, growing in dogs around the world. Canine transmissible venereal tumor (CTVT) is a single line of cancer cells passed from dog to dog as living cells, usually during mating, and it grows as tumors on the genitals.1

How do you date a cancer? Count its mutations. Some kinds of DNA change build up in cells at a roughly steady rate, so their total works like a clock. A 2014 study read the genomes of two tumors and estimated that the founder dog lived about 11,000 years ago, and that its cancer spread across continents only about 500 years ago.2 A larger 2019 study looked at 546 tumors from 43 countries, on every inhabited continent.3 Using a different mutation clock, it put the origin at roughly 4,000 to 8,500 years ago, probably in Central or Northern Asia, where the cancer then stayed for thousands of years.4 The clocks disagree, but either way these cells have outlived their first owner by millennia.

The tumors' family tree also tracks human history. By about 100 years ago the cancer was in dog populations worldwide, carried by people who moved dogs around the globe, probably by sea, between the 1400s and the early 1900s.5

concepts.title: Leukemia Adrift in the Sea
concepts.contentHtml:
Many shellfish, from clams and mussels to cockles and oysters, suffer from a leukemia-like cancer: cells multiply out of control in their hemolymph, the shellfish version of blood. Soft-shell clams on the east coast of North America have had it since at least the 1970s.1

In 2015, Michael Metzger, Stephen Goff and colleagues compared the DNA of the cancer cells with that of the clams carrying them. It did not match. Instead, cancer cells from clams in New York, Maine and Prince Edward Island in Canada were nearly identical to one another: a single clone, descended from one original clam, spreading from animal to animal.2

But how? Adult clams stay put and do not normally touch. They do filter feed, though, and each one pumps several liters of seawater an hour, so even a few drifting cancer cells could be enough.3 Later lab work showed that the cells survive well in seawater and that sick clams release them into the water.4

Clams were not alone. In 2016 the same group found contagious cancers in mussels, cockles and golden carpet shell clams, from lineages that had arisen separately. The oddest was in the golden carpet shell clams: their cancer cells were not golden carpet shell cells at all, but came from a different species, the pullet shell clam, living in the same area. A cancer had crossed from one species into another.5

title: Puppet Masters
description: Toxoplasma and fearless rats, a wasp that walks roaches on a leash, and crickets sent swimming

concepts.title: The Rat That Stopped Fearing Cats
concepts.contentHtml:
A healthy rat steers clear of places that carry signs of a cat, even if it has never met one. In a 2000 study, rats infected with the single-celled parasite Toxoplasma gondii lost much of that caution, and some were even drawn to cat-scented areas, while their other behavior and general health stayed normal.1

Why would a parasite want its rat eaten? Because of where it breeds. Toxoplasma can infect rats, but it reproduces sexually only in the gut of a cat. A 2007 study found that infected rats were attracted to cat urine instead of repelled by it, which may make a rat more likely to end up inside a cat, parasite and all.2

The story is famous, but its details are argued over. A 2020 study of mice found that infection made them less anxious and more exploratory in general, and blunted their avoidance of predators with no special focus on cats; the more parasite cysts in the brain, the bigger the change. Its authors called the selective loss of cat fear in mice a myth and pointed to the immune response in the brain instead.3

People catch it too. Over 40 million people in the United States carry Toxoplasma, and most healthy people never have symptoms.4 Studies have tied infection to mental illness and personality in people, but the findings conflict. A 2016 study of 837 adults from a long-running birth cohort in Dunedin, New Zealand, found no support for a link between infection and negative behavioral outcomes, and its authors called for better research designs.5

concepts.title: The Wasp That Walks a Roach
concepts.contentHtml:
The emerald jewel wasp, Ampulex compressa, hunts the American cockroach. She grabs the roach just behind the head and stings twice. The first sting goes into the nerve center in the thorax that controls the front legs, paralyzing them for a short while. The second goes through the soft neck and straight into the brain.1

What follows looks like obedience. The roach is not paralyzed, yet it lets the wasp snip off both its antennae and drink the fluid from the stumps. Then she grips one stump and pulls, and the roach follows her into a burrow on its own legs, walking normally, like a dog on a leash. She lays one egg on its leg and seals it in. The larva hatches, bores in and eats the roach's insides; about five days after the sting, the roach finally dies.2

The venom does not disable the muscles or the nerves that run them. It takes away the drive to move. A stung roach rarely walks on its own, but drop it in water and it swims, though it gives up much sooner than an unstung roach, as if it despairs faster.3

The textbook version is not the whole story. Filming the egg-laying up close, Kenneth Catania found in 2020 that the wasp usually stings three more times under the roach's thorax, apparently to shift a middle leg into the right position for her egg, and once more at the base of a front leg.4 And roaches can fight back. In his 2018 experiments, many fended off the wasp by raising their bodies to keep their necks out of reach and kicking at her head with their spiny hind legs.5

concepts.title: The Worm That Sends Crickets Swimming
concepts.contentHtml:
On summer nights near a forest in southern France, crickets turn up where crickets do not belong, out on bare concrete. Of 70 collected from such spots, 69 carried a parasite.1 Inside each was a horsehair worm, which grows from a microscopic larva into a worm three to four times bigger than its host.2

The worm needs water. Young hairworms live as parasites inside insects, but adults live free in water, where they mate and lay eggs. When the worm is mature, its host does something no healthy cricket does: it seeks out water and jumps in. The worm wriggles out into the water, and the host, if it does not drown, can live for months.3

How a worm steers an insect is only partly known. A 2005 study of grasshoppers carrying the hairworm Spinochordodes tellinii found that, during the manipulation, proteins linked to neurotransmitters changed in the host's brain, and the worm appeared to make proteins of the Wnt family that closely resemble insect ones, a possible case of molecular mimicry.4

The effects ripple through whole ecosystems. In a Japanese headwater stream, camel crickets and grasshoppers were 20 times more likely to enter the water if infected. Endangered Japanese trout ate so many of them that these insects supplied 60% of the trout population's yearly energy.5
